entities.name: Battle of Antietam
entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Battle of Antietam was a pivotal event in the American Civil War, fought on September 17, 1862, in Washington County, Maryland. It was the bloodiest single-day battle in American history, with over 22,000 casualties. The battle was a turning point in the war, as it halted the Confederate Army's invasion of the North and led to President Abraham Lincoln issuing the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring freedom for all slaves in Confederate territory. The consequences of the battle would be felt for generations to come, shaping the course of American history and cementing the Union's victory in the war.

The battle was a culmination of months of strategic maneuvering by both the Union and Confederate armies. General Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia had invaded the North, hoping to win a decisive victory on Union territory. However, General George McClellan's Union Army of the Potomac was determined to stop him. The two armies clashed on the banks of Antietam Creek, near the town of Sharpsburg, Maryland. The battle was a brutal and chaotic affair, with both sides suffering heavy losses. In the end, the Union army was able to drive the Confederates back across the Potomac River, but at a terrible cost in lives lost.

The Battle of Antietam was a significant turning point in the Civil War, marking a shift in momentum in favor of the Union. It led to a series of Union victories in the following months, ultimately contributing to the Confederacy's defeat. The battle also had a profound impact on the course of American history, setting the stage for the eventual abolition of slavery and the reunification of the nation.
